items.title: Vercel ships Vercel CI — skips unaffected tasks, 2-6x faster in their own repos
items.summary: Vercel CI reads your existing turbo.json: tag a task (e.g. tags: ["ci"] on lint) and it runs only on Vercel's Hive compute, sized to the push, with Remote Cache serving anything unchanged. Vercel reports 2-6x faster git-push-to-"CI passed" time in its own internal repos (its own measurement, not an independent benchmark). Inspectable via the Vercel CLI (vc ci ls/inspect/logs/grep) and the Vercel MCP server, and posts a normal GitHub check so branch protection still applies. In Beta, on all plans.
items.why: A CI that only reruns what a change actually touches, and that an agent can query through MCP instead of scraping logs, is the kind of plumbing that actually shortens an agentic dev loop.
items.action: Run `npx skills use vercel/ci@setup` on one repo with a turbo.json and tag your lint/test task for CI to see the cache-skip behavior firsthand.

items.title: Cursor ships Design Mode: Annotate — give agents visual edits instead of typed instructions
items.summary: In Cursor's browser Design Mode (Cmd+Shift+D), you can now draw directly on a page, edit elements inline, and review the layout at different screen sizes — then hand those visual annotations to an agent as the instruction, instead of describing the change in text.
items.why: A lot of UI feedback is easier to draw than to write ("move this 10px left, make this bigger") — letting an agent read visual annotations directly removes a translation step that usually loses precision.
items.action: Open a page in Cursor's browser, press Cmd+Shift+D, and annotate one real layout tweak before typing the equivalent instructions by hand — compare how much the agent gets right on the first try.

items.title: A durable task queue and workflow runtime that lives entirely in Postgres
items.summary: Marcelo Trylesinski (Pydantic/Starlette/Uvicorn maintainer) built pgtask: a queue, scheduler and durable workflow runtime with no broker and no extension — just PostgreSQL 16+. task.step() checkpoints a step's result so a retry resumes instead of restarting; task.sleep_for() and task.wait_for_signal() release the worker entirely, so a task asleep for six hours costs one database row, not a held worker slot. Pydantic AI agents run on it via PGTaskDurability, checkpointing every model request and tool call as its own step.
items.why: If an agent run crashes partway through a long tool-calling loop, a durable queue like this is what lets it resume from the last checkpoint instead of re-paying for every tool call it already made.
items.action: If you're running agent workflows that can crash or sleep mid-task (a human approval wait, a long external job), it's worth 10 minutes to see if PGTaskDurability fits your Spring Boot + Postgres stack more cheaply than a message-broker-based queue.

items.title: An engineer switched his production summarization pipeline to Liquid AI's new LFM3-1.7B
items.summary: Aditya Vivek Thota replaced Qwen3.5-4B with Liquid AI's just-shipped LFM3-1.7B for a local article-summarization workflow running 500+ items per run. LFM3 wins on instruction-following (IFEval 96.66 vs 92.52) and is roughly tied on long-context retrieval, while Qwen still leads on GPQA Diamond and 128K-context RULER — Liquid's own numbers, not an independent test. He reports over 100 tokens/sec and says the swap is already live in production as of today, with prompt tuning still in progress.
items.why: Real benchmarks are nice, but someone actually flipping a production workflow to a brand-new small model on day one, and saying why the tradeoffs were worth it, tells you more than the model's own announcement does.
items.action: If you have a local/edge inference step currently throttled by model size, LFM3-1.7B's roughly 1GB 4-bit footprint is worth a quick side-by-side against whatever you're running now.

eval.reason: First-hand production-adoption account of a brand-new model release, not a duplicate.

items.title: Inside a 10-person company spending 30x payroll on AI tokens, shipping 77,000 changes a month
items.summary: Jacob (@jsnnsa), founder of game studio Spawn, wrote up two years of restructuring the company around permanent AI agents ("the fleet") instead of short-lived coding sessions: no PRs (agents coordinate through shared state, "stigmergy"-style, instead of messaging each other), hourly deploys treated as a severe incident if missed, production testing instead of pre-merge suites, and AI judges that apply the founder's own past decisions to new ones (7,296 of about 11,000 judged automatically in the first 8 days). Only 0.9% of 123,548 changes have ever been reverted. Simon Willison called it "fascinating... my eyebrows raised at least a dozen times."
items.why: Most "agents writing code" stories are a demo; this is a founder describing, in detail, the actual engineering process changes — no PRs, hourly ship-or-it's-an-incident, AI judges for taste — that had to happen first, useful to study even if you'd only adopt pieces of it.
items.action: Read the "stigmergy" section specifically — agents coordinating through the shared state of the code/product instead of messaging each other is a concrete pattern you could prototype on a single service.

eval.reason: Detailed first-hand process writeup, not a pricing/funding/benchmark post; not a duplicate.

items.title: DeepLearning.AI and LangChain ship a course on the four loops behind reliable long-running agents
items.summary: "Loop Engineering with LangChain Deep Agents," taught by LangChain's Deep Agents maintainer Sydney Runkle with DeepLearning.AI's Esmaeil Gargari, breaks agent reliability into four loop types: the core agent loop (call tools, observe, decide), a verification loop (an evaluator checks output against a rubric and sends it back), an event-driven loop (triggered by a Slack message or Jira ticket), and a hill-climbing loop (analyzing traces across many runs to improve the harness itself). The hands-on example is a requirements-review agent using Deep Agents' filesystem, instructions and skills features.
items.why: The "hill-climbing loop" — using traces across runs to systematically improve the harness itself, not just the prompt — is exactly the kind of structural pattern that's easy to do ad hoc and hard to do rigorously, and this is a rare short course that names it directly.
items.action: Watch the verification-loop and hill-climbing-loop lessons specifically and compare their rubric-based verification pattern against however you currently grade your own harness's runs.

items.title: The four components Cole Medin says every AI second brain needs (Context, Connections, Capabilities, Cadence)
items.summary: Cole Medin lays out a deliberately simple second-brain stack (a few tools, a folder of markdown files) built around four fundamentals: Context (what the agent can see), Connections (what it's wired into), Capabilities (what it can actually do) and Cadence (how often it checks in) — framed as both a build guide and an audit checklist for a second brain you already have.
items.why: If you've already built an agent memory/second-brain setup and it feels like it's drifting or overbuilt, this gives you four concrete questions to audit it against instead of rebuilding from scratch.

items.title: How Anthropic scaled from 2,500 to 30,000 merged code changes a day
items.summary: Manish Kapur (Sonar) and Addy Osmani (Anthropic) discuss "light" vs. "dark" software factories, how Anthropic's own merge rate scaled 12x with Claude doing first-pass review backed by independent verification evidence (not just an LLM judge), new data from Sonar's State of Code survey, and a lightning round on when it's actually safe to merge agent-written PRs. Comments push back usefully — several viewers argue that counting merged PRs as a velocity metric hides how many are just fixes for previous agent-written bugs.
items.why: The core claim worth sitting with is that "coding is solved, confidence isn't" — the bottleneck moved from writing code to independently verifying it, the actual argument for investing in harness-level verification rather than a smarter model.
